summary: Trend Detective is a web tool that tests whether a variable measured by NASA Earth science missions and models is changing over time, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. The user picks a location, answers two short questions about the type of environment and the topic of interest, and receives suggested variables with plain-language definitions. The tool retrieves 45 years of monthly NASA POWER data (1981-2025), removes the seasonal cycle, plots the time series, estimates the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, and tests significance with both the Mann-Kendall test and a t-test. A trend is reported as significant only when both tests agree. A regional map tests a grid of points and shows where the same variable increases in one place and decreases in another, which the challenge identifies as a key difficulty. Users can also import NASA Giovanni time series (MODIS, OMI, AIRS, GPM, GLDAS) as CSV files. It is aimed at students and members of the public with some scientific background.
details:
What it does: For a chosen location and variable, the tool answers four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and is the change significant. Results appear as a chart, a plain-language verdict, and a table of statistics. A "Two-region comparison" view applies the same tests to two locations. A "Regional map" view tests a grid of 16 to 49 points around the chosen location, colours each point by its rate of change, and marks the points that are significant, so users can see regions moving in opposite directions. An "Import data" view analyses CSV time series downloaded from NASA Giovanni.

How it works: (1) Monthly values for 1981-2025 are retrieved from the NASA POWER API at the chosen coordinates. (2) The long-term mean for each calendar month is subtracted to remove the seasonal cycle. (3) One value is computed per complete year. (4) The rate of change is estimated with Sen's slope and with ordinary least squares, each with a 95% confidence interval. (5) Significance is tested with the Mann-Kendall test and a two-sided t-test on the slope; a trend is called significant only if both give p below 0.05. (6) The lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals is calculated, and a warning is shown when it is high, because it makes p-values too small. The statistical routines were checked against SciPy on a test series.

Example results from live NASA POWER data: air temperature at Boston shows a significant increase of about 0.43 degrees C per decade over 1981-2025; at Utqiagvik in Arctic Alaska about 0.64 degrees C per decade; aerosol optical depth over Beijing shows a significant decrease of about 0.11 per decade since 2001.

Benefits: It lets non-specialists test a trend properly instead of judging a line on a chart, and it states what the numbers do and do not show. The Method page lists the limitations: the data are gridded model and satellite products with a resolution of roughly 50 km, only linear trends are tested, a significant trend does not identify its cause, and when many map points are tested about 1 in 20 can look significant by chance.

What I hope to achieve: a classroom and public tool for learning how scientists decide that a change is real. Planned next steps: add GPM, GLDAS and MODIS data directly, add trend tests that allow for autocorrelation, and add worked classroom exercises.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML and CSS (single page, no server), Plotly.js for charts and maps, NASA POWER API for data. Statistical checks were run in Python with SciPy.

Live tool: https://adam-nite.github.io/NASA-Challenge/ | Code: https://github.com/adam-nite/NASA-Challenge
